introduction.heading: What is JavaScript?
introduction.description: JavaScript is the language that runs in every browser and, via Node.js, on servers too - it's how a page reacts to clicks, fetches data, and updates itself without a full reload. It's dynamically typed (a variable can hold any kind of value), runs your code top to bottom on a single thread, and leans on functions and closures more than classes to organize logic. Everything else in this app - TypeScript, React, Node, Redux - is JavaScript with something layered on top, so the concepts here are the foundation for all of it.

concepts.title: Variables & Scope
concepts.description: var is function-scoped and hoisted to the top of its function; let and const are block-scoped and unreachable before their declaration line runs

concepts.title: Functions & Closures
concepts.description: A function remembers the variables that were in scope where it was defined, even after the outer function that created it has already returned

concepts.title: Arrays & Objects
concepts.description: Ordered lists and named fields, the two building blocks for structured data - methods like map, filter, and reduce transform them without a manual loop

concepts.title: Destructuring & Spread/Rest
concepts.description: Pull values out of an array or object by position or name with destructuring, or go the other way and expand/collect values with the same ... syntax

concepts.title: Template Literals
concepts.description: Backtick strings that embed real expressions with ${...} and can span multiple lines, replacing most manual string concatenation

concepts.title: Promises & Async/Await
concepts.description: A Promise represents a value that isn't ready yet; async/await is syntax that lets promise-based code read top-to-bottom like synchronous code

eventLoop.heading: The Event Loop, Briefly
eventLoop.description: JavaScript itself is single-threaded - only one line of your code runs at a time. Asynchronous work like timers, network requests, and promises doesn't block that thread; it's handed off, and the callback comes back through a queue once your current code finishes. Promises jump ahead of timers, so a resolved .then() always runs before a setTimeout(fn, 0), even though both are "async".

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: Open your browser's DevTools console (or run node in a terminal) and start typing - no build step or install required
Declare variables with const by default, and let only when you know you'll reassign it; avoid var in new code
Reach for array methods - map, filter, reduce, find - before reaching for a manual for loop
Destructure function parameters and returned objects instead of reaching into them field by field
Use template literals (`Hello ${name}`) instead of string concatenation with +
Prefer async/await over raw .then() chains once you have more than one dependent asynchronous step

fullExample.heading: Full Example, Step by Step
fullExample.title: A task tracker: closures, spread/rest, destructuring, and async/await
fullExample.description: This ties the core concepts above together in one realistic file: a closure keeping private state, rest and spread keeping updates immutable, a template literal for output, and an async function that awaits inside a loop. Click through the steps to see which lines each one is talking about.
code: const task = { id: tasks.length + 1, title, tags, done: false };
tasks = tasks.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: true } : t));

steps.label: Close over local state
steps.explanation: tasks is declared inside createTaskTracker and never exposed directly - the object returned on line 4 keeps referencing it after the outer function has finished running. That's a closure.

steps.label: Collect extra arguments with rest
steps.explanation: ...tags gathers every argument after title into a real array, so add("Ship it", "urgent", "code") ends up with tags = ["urgent", "code"].

steps.label: Add without mutating the original array
steps.explanation: [...tasks, task] builds a brand-new array instead of pushing onto the old one in place, so nothing else holding a reference to the previous tasks array gets surprised by a change.

steps.label: Update one item without mutating it
steps.explanation: map returns a new array, and { ...t, done: true } copies every field off the matching task and overrides just done, leaving the original task object untouched.

steps.label: Destructure and interpolate
steps.explanation: const { length } = tasks pulls a single named field off an object; the template literal `${done}/${length} tasks done` embeds both values directly into the string.

steps.label: Await inside a loop
steps.explanation: for...of combined with await pauses each iteration until fetch and response.json() resolve, and const { title } destructures the field straight out of the resolved JSON.

steps.label: Use the closure
steps.explanation: tracker holds a tasks array no outside code can touch directly - every read or write here goes through add, complete, or summary, exactly the API the closure was built to expose.
